newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Deutsche Boerse looks to EMU for new business.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Boerse looks to EMU for new business.

text.p: Preparation for European Monetary Union (EMU) is running "according to plan," said Joerg Franke, a senior member of the executive board of Deutsche Boerse.
Speaking to reporters during an annual meeting of futures industry officials here which ended Saturday, Franke said German equity markets should draw more investment as a result of EMU.
"The German stock market will probably get a boost from European Monetary Union," he said.
Deutsche Boerse is the operating company for Germany's largest stock exchange based in Frankfurt, and also for the futures and options exchange Deutsche Terminboerse (DTB).
Much of the new business generated by EMU is expected to be in equities products.
DTB will launch a futures contract based on a DAX mid-cap index on September 23, along with 19 stock options, bringing the number of options listed on the electronic exchange to 39.

It will also list options on Deutsche Telekom, the telecommunications arm of the German post and telecom authority. Telekom is slated for flotation in November. DTB hopes to list the options just a day after the stock offering.
Speaking to reporters Thursday, Franke said the focus with EMU was likely to be more "sectoral than national." Thus, German exchanges may consider offering equity products based on sector indices.

It is more difficult to foresee what will happen to debt products, given that interest rates of the countries joining EMU would be expected to converge as a single "euro" currency is phased in. The shift to EMU is due to start in 1999.
Much of the competition for such products is expected in very short-term interest rate products.

DTB could be ready early next year to launch a three-month mark contract. The contract would compete with the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange's (LIFFE) three-month mark contract based on LIBOR (London Interbank Offered Rate), Franke said.
At the same time the German futures exchange would delist its FIBOR (Frankfurt Interbank Offered Rate) contract which is virtually inactive.
In the U.S., Franke said DTB will install two "access points" in Chicago in late September for two of its members. By year-end, a total of six access points are expected to be connected in the U.S.

Such points allow DTB members in the U.S. direct access to trade on DTB, a fully electronic exchange. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has granted DTB a no-action letter clearing the way for U.S. trade in its debt futures products.
Deutsche Boerse will now seek similar permission from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to allow links for equity products, including those based on the German DAX index.
